content: The Loud and Proud campaign, spearheaded by Youth Voices Count, is a regional advocacy initiative aimed at addressing self-stigma and its connection to HIV vulnerabilities among young men who have sex with men (MSM) and young transgender individuals in Asia. This campaign was implemented in four countries—Indonesia, Mongolia, the Philippines, and Vietnam—and included in-country activities, community-friendly events, and the production of four short videos. The campaign sought to promote self-acceptance, self-confidence, and health-seeking behaviors while advocating for timely psychosocial services for these populations. It also empowered young MSM and transgender individuals to use multimedia platforms and social networks for advocacy. The HIV Cooperation Programme for Indonesia (HCPI) supported training programs focused on Positive Prevention, aiming to empower people living with HIV (PLHIV) by enhancing their self-esteem, confidence, and ability to lead healthier lives while reducing their risk of infections. A collaborative team of seven individuals from national networks of PLHIV and key populations developed facilitator training materials based on their experiences. These facilitators were trained to integrate the acquired knowledge and skills into peer support groups and NGO programs. The training materials targeted people who inject drugs, sex workers (male, female, and transgender), and their partners, as well as men who buy sex and their partners. The modules covered topics such as HIV and STI prevention, disclosure of HIV status, adherence to antiretroviral therapy, and coping with discrimination. External experts reviewed the modules, which were field-tested and launched in 2012. Fifty-four individuals from 23 provinces, mostly from key populations, were trained using these modules, along with materials on sexual and reproductive health and facilitation skills. In Indonesia, the Fokus Muda program promotes the meaningful involvement of young key populations in the HIV response and broader sexual health and rights initiatives. It brings together young people aged 15–27 for advocacy, capacity building, and technical assistance, helping them become effective leaders in representing their communities. The program conducted consultations and capacity-building sessions with young people who inject drugs, sell sex, have sex with men, are transgender, or live with HIV. These sessions were tailored to the unique profiles and interests of each group. Participants represented local community-based organizations and had been actively engaged in their communities for at least one year. A national consultation meeting encouraged participants to identify their most pressing issues, such as the lack of services specific to their needs and harm-reduction programming for young people who inject drugs. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) launched the Global Commission on HIV and the Law in 2010 to develop actionable, evidence-based recommendations for an HIV response that protects and promotes the human rights of PLHIV and those vulnerable to HIV. In Uruguay, a national inter-sectoral commission was organized to harmonize and improve national legislation related to the HIV response. This initiative, supported by UNDP, UNFPA, and UNAIDS, provided a platform for affected individuals and civil society organizations to present evidence of human rights violations, including issues related to sexual orientation, gender identity, discrimination in health services, employment, education, police brutality, and access to treatment. The dialogue contributed to the development of a comprehensive HIV law, with recommendations presented to parliament in 2014. The Metropolitan Community Church of New York (MCCNY) Homeless Youth Services provides emergency housing for LGBTQI youth aged 18–24, integrated with supportive services such as HIV testing and counseling, mental health care, medical care, syringe access, case management, anti-violence education, and job training. Programs are developed in response to client feedback, ensuring services meet their needs. For example, after transgender participants expressed a need for reliable access to health services, the program arranged for on-site enrollment in Medicaid benefits and partnered with an HIV/AIDS coalition to provide hormone therapy without waiting lists. In 2013, the program assisted over 200 LGBTQI homeless youth in accessing housing and provided HIV testing and referrals for 145 clients. Streetwise and Safe (SAS) empowers LGBTQQ youth of color aged 16–24 who experience criminalization, including those involved in selling sex. SAS conducts know your rights workshops tailored to LGBTQQ youth, providing legal information and strategies to reduce harm during interactions with police and the court system. SAS also creates opportunities for youth to participate in policy discussions and advocate for their rights. The organization has led campaigns to end discriminatory stop and frisk practices and the use of condoms as evidence in prostitution-related offenses. In 2014, the New York City Police Department announced it would discontinue using condoms as evidence in certain offenses, though SAS continues to push for broader policy changes. The Centre for the Development of People (CEDEP) in Malawi addresses the needs of minority populations, including men who have sex with men (MSM), in a context of homophobia and criminalization. CEDEP peer educators mobilize MSM through snowballing techniques and advocate for non-discriminatory health services. Sensitization of health providers and stakeholders has improved access to and quality of HIV services for MSM. As of 2014, CEDEP trained 80 peer educators, leading to greater community mobilization and partnerships with health services.
